questions.q: Which of these is a real way to sort databases into types?
options: By the shape of the data, like tables, documents, links or readings
By where it runs, like cloud or on-premises
By whether it is free or paid
By how old the product is
questions.explain: The post sorts by data shape and by workload. "Cloud database" describes where it runs, not how it stores data, so it is not a type.

questions.q: You run a shop and need to store orders and billing records, where the rules across records must always hold. Where does the post say to start?
questions.explain: Microsoft's choice table sends strict multi-entity transactions to relational. The post says to add a specialist when an access pattern clearly diverges.

questions.q: A search engine is great for full-text queries, relevance scores and fuzzy matching. Why shouldn't it be the one place your data lives?
options: It can only hold numbers, never text
It is slow at finding words
It only works with data about links between people
Its index can lag behind the latest changes, so keep the source of truth somewhere else
questions.explain: Search indexes are eventually consistent, which means they can trail behind. The post says to keep the source of truth somewhere else and let search sit on top.

questions.q: The post says PostgreSQL, Redis and Google Spanner each cover more than one type. So what should you shop by?
options: The product with the most famous name
Always a separate database for every job
questions.explain: Labels blur, so start from the job. Before adding a new database, check whether the one you already run does the job well enough.
